commons:98691695.summary: Against a golden ground, Christ stands in white and gold within a blue almond-shaped mandorla, rays of light streaming from him. The prophets Elijah and Moses, named in Greek, stand on either side, while below John and James start back on their knees and Peter lies prostrate at Christ's feet, overwhelmed by the light. A border of medallions with busts of apostles and prophets frames the apse. Set above the altar at the foot of Mount Sinai, where Moses met God, it is the earliest surviving example of the standard Byzantine image of the Transfiguration.
facts: It dates from the time of, and was probably commissioned by, Emperor Justinian, who founded the monastery late in his reign.
It contains the earliest extant Transfiguration mandorla; at this date only Christ is given a halo.
The subject had a special meaning at Sinai because of the meeting of Christ with Moses, the site's own great prophet; the monastery's patronal feast is the Transfiguration.

commons:98691695.notes: Commons gives 'circa 600'; Wikipedia places it in Justinian's reign. In this photograph the inscriptions name Elijah at viewer's left and Moses at right, whereas Wikipedia's text says the reverse; the description follows the visible labels.

Q1748749.summary: The lid of this reliquary of the True Cross is set with nine enamel panels framed by gems and pearls. In the centre Christ sits enthroned between the Virgin and St John the Baptist, a Deesis flanked by the archangels Gabriel and Michael, while the rows above and below hold the twelve apostles. Inside lies a double-armed cross containing fragments of the True Cross, so that the lid presents Christ in glory over the relic of his Passion.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the cross inside names the emperors Constantine VII and Romanos II, who ruled jointly from 945 to 959, while the box was made later for Basil Lekapenos, probably between 963 and 985.
Compartments around the cross held ten further relics, among them the swaddling clothes and crown of thorns of Christ, belts of the Virgin and hair of John the Baptist.
It was probably brought to Germany as loot from the Fourth Crusade and is now in the Diocesan Museum at Limburg an der Lahn; the box measures 48 × 38 cm.
Q1748749.notes: Box date changed from 'c. 964–965' to Wikipedia's 'probably 963–985' (between Basil's elevation to proedros and his exile).

Q116273033.summary: Christ stands rather than hangs on the cross, his arms stretched straight and his feet planted on a patterned footrest, while two half-length angels mourn above the cross-arm. Below, the Virgin wraps herself in her mantle in grief and John, holding a book, lifts his hand toward his Lord. Made in Amalfi around 1060–70, the plaque shows the strong Byzantine influence in the ivories of southern Italy.
facts: The Met suggests that the plaque probably served as the central panel of a triptych icon.
It is about 12.9 × 8.6 cm and was given to the Met by J. Pierpont Morgan in 1917.
